messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo Alvarez was 35 when a late-night freeway crash left him convinced that the life he had been living as a working musician had been split into a before and an after. He had been driving home after a gig with his equipment in the back seat when another car came across lanes at high speed and struck the driver’s side. He remembered the violent sideways jolt, the scream of metal, the smell of something burning, and then only scattered images: glass across his lap, a horn blaring without stopping, red lights flashing somewhere beyond the windshield. What stayed with him was not a clear story but a set of broken pieces, and from the beginning that missingness mattered to him. He had come to feel that something enormous and irreversible had been taken from him in a moment that was deeply unfair, and because no complete account in his own mind seemed available, the accident felt unfinished, as if the worst of it might still be waiting in the parts he could not reach.

In the weeks afterward, Mateo found that whenever he tried to deliberately remember the crash, his mind did not produce a continuous sequence. Instead, isolated fragments came up and then disappeared: the impact, a stranger’s face leaning toward him, his own hand shaking, then nothing. He would sit with the effort to piece it together and feel defeated by how incomplete it was. That broken quality fed what he already feared about the accident’s meaning. If he could not even hold the event in a whole form, it seemed to confirm for him that his life had been wrecked in a way he could not master or make sense of. The gaps also frightened him for another reason: he was certain that if he ever accessed the whole memory, the anger he carried about the injustice of what had happened would flood out of him and he might not be able to control it.

Those beliefs shaped how he began living. Mateo did not want to be alone with his thoughts, because being alone made space for the crash to press at the edges of his mind and for his anger to gather. He started arranging his days so that someone was always around. If he was not rehearsing, he was calling bandmates, lingering after sets, finding reasons to meet friends for food or drinks, or sitting at his brother’s apartment long after he wanted to go home. His wife noticed that he resisted any quiet evening in their apartment. He told himself that staying in company was safer; if he kept conversation going, he would not have to think about what happened, and he would not risk saying aloud how cheated and ruined he felt.

His work as a musician gave this strategy an easy cover. In studios, backstage, and in bars after performances, Mateo could remain surrounded by people without seeming avoidant even to himself. But the habit hardened. When another musician casually asked about the accident, he would shrug, make a joke, or turn the conversation back to gear or set lists. He avoided talking about the crash or about the months after it with almost rehearsed skill. The less he spoke about it and the more completely he pushed away attempts to think about it, the less accessible the memory seemed to become. When he tested himself privately—trying to recall the sequence from leaving the venue to the ambulance—he got only disconnected pieces again, and that failure made him retreat even more quickly into noise, company, and distraction.

Over months, the cycle tightened. Because the memory remained fractured and hard to deliberately retrieve, Mateo treated his own mind as dangerous territory. He believed that whatever was missing contained something that would prove just how thoroughly the accident had destroyed his life, or ignite a rage he could not contain. To prevent that, he kept himself busy and socially saturated, but this constant socialising meant he almost never stayed still long enough to let the memory settle into a fuller narrative. In session he described it as “keeping the speakers on” so he would not hear what was underneath. Yet the consequence was that what lay underneath never became clearer; it stayed jagged and incomplete, which in turn left his sense of injustice raw and his view of the future bleak.

His marriage had begun to narrow around these habits. His wife wanted to understand what had changed in him, but Mateo would not talk about the crash and could not explain why he came home from gigs only to call someone else or invite people over. She experienced him as absent even when he was physically there. He experienced home as intolerably quiet. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the effort it took to keep himself constantly occupied and frightened by how much power the missing pieces still held. What finally brought him in was the recognition that he could no longer imagine getting his life back by outrunning his thoughts. He said he was most afraid that if he stopped, the anger would take over; he was also beginning, cautiously, to hope that if the story of the crash could become less broken, his life might not be as permanently destroyed as he had come to believe.
